title: When the Aftermath Burns
premise: Bram Blackwood, a night librarian who has spent eleven years erasing herself after a fire killed her best friend and songwriter Juniper Vale, hears an unreleased song—written only for her—playing on a late-night radio show. The broadcast is a message: someone from the old circle, the band that burned with their dreams in a farmhouse outside Marrow Creek, is dying and wants to confess what really happened that night. Returning home, Bram must untangle whether the fire was accident, arson, or sacrifice, while the town's silence protects a man she once loved. In the end, Bram chooses testimony over vengeance, giving Juniper's song back to the world under its true name—and finally claiming her own.
about_author: W. M. Underhill is the pen name of a former small-town radio archivist who spent years cataloguing tapes no one claimed. When the Aftermath Burns is their first novel, drawn from the strange intimacy of voices left behind on magnetic tape.

chapters.title: The Hours That Belong to No One
chapters.summary: POV Bram. A portrait of Bram's nocturnal routine at the Halloway Branch Library: shelving, avoiding patrons, perfecting the smile that ends conversations. She catalogs a donation of old cassettes without listening. Emotional beat: loneliness worn as armor; the reader senses a life built to prevent feeling.

chapters.title: A Song With No Name
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Closing the library at dawn, Bram hears a late-night radio program play a melody she knows intimately—one Juniper wrote for her alone, never recorded. The DJ credits it as 'anonymous, found tape.' Emotional beat: shock cracking open eleven years of carefully sealed grief; her hands shake on the steering wheel.

chapters.title: What the Tape Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Bram plays the donated cassettes and finds rehearsal recordings from the band's Marrow Creek days—Juniper's voice, laughter, and a date stamp three days before the fire. Someone mailed them deliberately. Emotional beat: dread braided with longing; evidence arriving like a summons.

chapters.title: The Smile Fails
chapters.summary: POV Bram. At work, a patron recognizes Bram from an old local news photo of the fire. Her practiced smile collapses; she flees mid-shift. Her supervisor, Odile, a dry-witted widow, covers for her and asks one question: 'Who did you used to be?' Emotional beat: identity as performance failing publicly.

chapters.title: Marrow Creek on the Map Again
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Bram researches the radio DJ—Cass Merrow, formerly of the band—and learns he returned to Marrow Creek last year and now hosts from a low-power station in his barn. She buys a bus ticket she doesn't yet use. Emotional beat: the pull of return versus the terror of being known.

chapters.title: Odile's Kitchen
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Odile feeds Bram soup and extracts the story in fragments: the band, the farmhouse, Juniper, the fire ruled accidental, the man Bram loved—Theo Vance—who inherited everything and stayed. Odile says, 'Grief you don't examine becomes a tenant.' Emotional beat: found family beginning; first honest tears in years.

chapters.title: Arrival
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Bram arrives in Marrow Creek, a town half-gentrified, half-rotted. The farmhouse ruins are fenced off, slated for demolition in three weeks—the same deadline ticking beneath Cass's broadcasts. She sees Theo across the square, older, respected, running the town's development office. Emotional beat: vertigo of return; the past physically smaller and more menacing than memory.

chapters.title: The Barn Station
chapters.summary: POV Cass. Cass, dying of a heart condition he hides, explains via narration why he plays the tapes: he found Juniper's diary in the farmhouse debris years ago and has been waiting for courage or death, whichever came first. He spots Bram listening outside his fence. Emotional beat: guilt as slow poison; two cowards recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Juniper's Diary
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Cass gives Bram the water-damaged diary. Entries reveal Juniper knew the band's manager, Dell Harrow, was stealing royalties, and that she planned to confront him the week of the fire. The last entry is torn out. Emotional beat: the friend Bram mourned was sharper, angrier, more alive than the saint she'd enshrined.

chapters.title: Theo Vance, Citizen of the Year
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Bram engineers a run-in with Theo at the historical society. He is warm, wounded-seeming, and insists the fire haunts him too. But he flinches when she mentions Dell Harrow—a name absent from every account. Emotional beat: charm as camouflage; Bram unsure whether she's interviewing a witness or a suspect.

chapters.title: Dell Harrow's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Tracking Dell through county records, Bram finds he died two years ago—but his sister, Ruthie, kept his files. Among them: royalty statements showing the band was owed thousands, and a threatening letter from Juniper dated the day before the fire. Emotional beat: justice outside the law taking shape as Bram realizes the legal system already failed here once.

chapters.title: Ruthie
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Ruthie Harrow, blunt and unafraid, tells Bram that Dell confessed to her before dying: he was at the farmhouse that night, saw someone leave through the back, and took money to stay silent. She won't say who paid until Bram proves she can be trusted. Emotional beat: alliance forged between two people the town discarded.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: POV Cass. Cass admits he tore out the diary's final page years ago because it named Theo—not as an arsonist, but as the person Juniper trusted with her confrontation plan. His shame: protecting Theo to protect himself from complicity. Emotional beat: confession as relief and betrayal at once; the midpoint reversal.

chapters.title: What Bram Did That Night
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Flashback chapter: the truth of Bram's guilt. She left the farmhouse early after fighting with Juniper about leaving the band—and locked the side door against intruders, a habit from city life, which may have trapped whoever started the fire. Emotional beat: devastating self-reckoning; her invisibility revealed as penance.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Development Office
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Bram confronts Theo with the ledger and diary. He breaks: Dell confronted him that night demanding hush money over the stolen royalties; they fought; a lamp overturned; Theo fled and let the fire spread rather than call it in and be questioned. He didn't kill her—but he let her burn. Emotional beat: climax of revelation; evil shown as cowardice compounded.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Theo offers Bram anything—money, the farmhouse land preserved as a memorial, public tribute to Juniper—if she stays silent. He invokes their old love. Bram, tempted by the memorial that would enshrine Juniper forever, must choose. Emotional beat: the seduction of a beautiful lie; the book's moral crux.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: POV Cass. Cass, worsening fast, broadcasts Juniper's full song on air and names it: 'Aftermath.' The town listens; old wounds reopen; Ruthie comes forward publicly about Dell. Theo's lawyer calls Bram with threats. Emotional beat: rising action cresting; the town forced to remember what it agreed to forget.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Bram gives her statement to a reopened inquiry, including her own role—the locked door—even though it exposes her to charges. Theo is arrested for obstruction and involuntary manslaughter. Emotional beat: costly integrity; justice chosen over safety, and self-forgiveness still out of reach.

chapters.title: The Farmhouse, Before It Falls
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Granted access before demolition, Bram walks the ruin and finds, charred but legible, lyrics Juniper had nailed inside the piano—verses meant for Bram, forgiving her in advance for whatever she'd blame herself for. Emotional beat: catharsis; grief transmuted into inheritance.

chapters.title: Sentencing
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Theo receives his sentence; he asks Bram to visit someday, and she neither promises nor refuses. Bram faces minor consequences for the door and accepts them without drama. Ruthie and Cass stand with her on the courthouse steps. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; the law doing only part of the work, the rest done by truth-telling.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: POV Bram. Back at the Halloway Branch, Bram catalogues Juniper's recovered recordings properly, under her name, and plays them over the library's evening hours for anyone who wanders in. Strangers linger. Odile brings soup. Emotional beat: found family consolidating; invisibility exchanged for presence.

chapters.title: The Song Under Its True Name
chapters.summary: POV Bram, closing outward. A year later: the farmhouse site is a small garden and listening bench; Cass's station continues under Ruthie's stewardship; Bram teaches a night writing class for insomniacs and signs her full name to the register. On air, 'Aftermath' plays, credited to Juniper Vale, 'for B.' Emotional beat: identity reclaimed; the aftermath no longer burning but blooming.
